title: Constituents and Phrase Structure
description: How words group into phrases and phrases into sentences

concepts.title: What Is a Constituent?
concepts.contentHtml:
A constituent is a group of words that behaves as a single unit within a sentence. Not every sequence of adjacent words is a constituent.

Tests for constituency include:

  • Substitution: can a single word replace the group? 'The big red dog' → 'it' (yes = constituent)
  • Movement: can the group move to the front? 'The book, I read.' (book = constituent)
  • Question fragment: can it answer a question by itself? 'What did she buy?' → 'A new car.' (yes = constituent)

Constituency is fundamental: syntactic rules apply to constituents, not to arbitrary strings of words. Understanding constituency is step one in parsing any sentence.

concepts.title: Phrase Structure — NP, VP, PP
concepts.contentHtml:
Sentences consist of phrases, each headed by a particular word class:

  • NP (Noun Phrase): 'the old man', 'my coffee' — head is a noun
  • VP (Verb Phrase): 'ate the cake', 'will arrive soon' — head is a verb
  • PP (Prepositional Phrase): 'in the garden', 'after lunch' — head is a preposition
  • AP (Adjective Phrase): 'very tall', 'proud of her work'

These phrases combine hierarchically: a sentence = NP + VP; a VP can contain an NP; an NP can contain a PP. The result is a nested structure — a tree, not a chain.

concepts.title: Heads and Their Complements
concepts.contentHtml:
Every phrase has a head — the central element that determines the phrase's category and requirements. The head selects its complement: what must accompany it.

A transitive verb like eat selects a direct object NP: 'eat the cake'. A preposition like in requires a following NP: 'in the garden'. Violation of selection restrictions sounds wrong: *'She arrived the book.'

The X-bar schema (introduced in generative grammar) formalizes this: every phrase has a head X, an optional specifier (XP → Spec X'), and optional complements (X' → X Complement). This captures why phrase structure is remarkably similar across different word classes.

title: Grammatical Relations and Word Order
description: Subjects, objects, and how languages express them

concepts.title: Subject, Object, Predicate
concepts.contentHtml:
Every clause has grammatical relations — the roles its noun phrases play:

  • Subject: typically the topic or agent — 'The dog bit the man.'
  • Direct Object: typically the patient or theme — 'The dog bit the man.'
  • Indirect Object: recipient — 'She gave him the book.'

Languages mark grammatical relations differently. English mainly uses word order: subject precedes verb, object follows. Latin uses case endings instead: canis hominem mordet (dog-NOM man-ACC bites) — 'the dog bites the man', regardless of word order.

concepts.title: Basic Word Order Typology
concepts.contentHtml:
Greenberg (1963) surveyed world languages and found that the relative order of Subject (S), Verb (V), and Object (O) clusters into a few types:

  • SVO: English, Mandarin, Swahili — 'I eat rice'
  • SOV: Japanese, Turkish, Hindi — 'I rice eat'
  • VSO: Arabic, Welsh, Classical Hebrew — 'Eat I rice'
  • SOV and SVO account for ~85% of languages

Word order correlates with other features: SOV languages tend to have postpositions (after the noun), whereas SVO languages tend to have prepositions (before the noun). These typological correlates reveal deep patterning.

concepts.title: Passive Voice and Grammatical Transformations
concepts.contentHtml:
The passive promotes the object to subject position and demotes or removes the agent: 'The dog bit the man' → 'The man was bitten by the dog.'

Cross-linguistically, passives serve similar pragmatic functions — foregrounding the affected entity, backgrounding or omitting the agent. Japanese passive has an additional 'adversative' reading: watashi wa ame ni fur-are-ta (I was rained on) — something bad happened to me, the rain didn't 'choose' to act.

Chomsky's early transformational grammar described passive as a transformation from an underlying active structure. Modern minimalism treats it differently, but the core insight — that surface subject ≠ deep semantic agent — remains central to syntax.

title: Chomsky and Generative Grammar
description: The theory that reshaped linguistics — universal grammar and recursion

concepts.title: The Chomskyan Revolution
concepts.contentHtml:
Before Noam Chomsky's Syntactic Structures (1957), linguistics was primarily descriptive and behaviorist. Chomsky argued that human language cannot be learned from input alone — children acquire grammar too fast and accurately for mere imitation.

His key proposal: all humans share an innate Universal Grammar (UG) — a biological blueprint specifying the possible structures of any human language. Children don't learn grammar from scratch; they set parameters on this shared template.

Chomsky distinguished competence (a speaker's internalized grammatical knowledge) from performance (actual language use, subject to memory limits and error). Linguistics, he argued, should study competence.

concepts.title: Recursion and Infinite Sentences
concepts.contentHtml:
One of Chomsky's central insights: human language is discrete infinity. From a finite set of words and rules, we can produce and understand infinitely many sentences.

The key mechanism is recursion: structures can embed copies of themselves. 'I think [that she knows [that he believes [that...]]]]' — there is no longest grammatical sentence.

Parse trees show recursion visually — an NP can contain a relative clause which contains another NP which contains another relative clause. English sentence embedding, Japanese postpositional phrases, Swahili complement clauses — all recursive.

Hauser, Chomsky and Fitch (2002) controversially proposed that recursion may be the only uniquely human component of the language faculty (the 'faculty of language in the narrow sense', FLN). This claim remains debated.

concepts.title: Parse Trees and Phrase Markers
concepts.contentHtml:
A parse tree (phrase marker) visualizes the hierarchical structure of a sentence. Each node is labeled with a category; branching shows constituency.

'The cat ate the fish' parses as:
S → NP VP
NP → Det N ('the cat')
VP → V NP
NP → Det N ('the fish')

Trees capture structural ambiguity: 'I saw the man with the telescope' has two trees — was the telescope used to see, or did the man have it? The same words yield two different trees with different meanings. This is structural (syntactic) ambiguity — impossible to capture in a linear string.

title: Movement, Dependencies, and Long-Distance Relations
description: How elements move and leave traces in syntactic structure

concepts.title: Wh-Movement and Questions
concepts.contentHtml:
In English questions, the question word moves to the front: 'What did she eat?' The 'what' originated as the object of 'eat' — 'she ate what' — and moved to the front. Generative syntax posits an abstract trace or copy in the original position.

Evidence for movement: 'island constraints' restrict where you can move from. 'What did she buy a book about?' is OK — 'what' moves from object of 'about'. But *'What did she buy a book about a theory that explains?' is grammatically blocked — you cannot extract from inside a relative clause (a 'complex NP island'). These constraints operate on structure, not linear position.

concepts.title: Head-Final vs Head-Initial Languages
concepts.contentHtml:
In head-initial languages like English, the head comes before its complement: verb before object ('eat the cake'), preposition before NP ('in the garden').

In head-final languages like Japanese and Turkish, the head follows its complement: object before verb ('cake-o tabe-ru'), postposition after NP ('garden-ni').

This parameter — head-initial vs head-final — correlates with many other properties: complement-clause structure, question-word placement, relative clause order. The head-directionality parameter was one of the classic parameters in Chomsky's Principles and Parameters model of UG: set one switch and many facts about a language fall into place.

concepts.title: Anaphora and Binding Theory
concepts.contentHtml:
Binding theory governs how pronouns and reflexives relate to their antecedents within sentence structure.

Principle A: A reflexive (himself, herself) must be bound (have an antecedent) in its local clause. 'John hurt himself' — himself refers to John. *'John said Bill hurt himself' (himself cannot refer back to John across the clause boundary).

Principle B: A pronoun must be free (not bound) in its local clause. 'John hurt him' — him cannot refer to John. 'John said Bill hurt him' — him can refer to John.

Similar constraints recur across typologically diverse languages, which generativists take as support for a universal grammatical architecture (though long-distance reflexives, such as Mandarin ziji, complicate Principle A).

title: Cross-Linguistic Syntax and Contemporary Debates
description: Ergative languages, discourse-configurationality, and the limits of UG

concepts.title: Ergative–Absolutive Languages
concepts.contentHtml:
Most linguistic theory is built on nominative–accusative languages like English, where the subject of a transitive verb and the subject of an intransitive verb receive the same case (nominative). The object gets accusative.

Ergative–absolutive languages work differently: the subject of a transitive verb (the agent) gets ergative case, while the subject of an intransitive verb and the object of a transitive verb both get absolutive case. The grouping is agent vs non-agent, not subject vs object.

Examples: Basque, many Australian languages, Tibetan, many Mayan languages. Ergativity challenged early universalist claims and forced syntacticians to rethink the definition of 'subject'.

concepts.title: Topic-Prominent Languages
concepts.contentHtml:
Li and Thompson (1976) proposed a distinction between subject-prominent languages (English, most European) and topic-prominent languages (Mandarin, Japanese, Korean).

In Mandarin, the topic — what the sentence is about — may be grammatically central even if it is not the agent: Nèi běn shū wǒ yǐjīng kàn-guo-le 'That book, I have already read' — the book is topic and appears first, though the subject is 'I'. Double nominative constructions in Japanese ('As for elephants, noses are long') have a topic that is not even a grammatical argument.

Topic-prominence shows that not all languages organize their grammar around the same primitives as English.

concepts.title: Minimalism and the Poverty of the Stimulus
concepts.contentHtml:
Chomsky's Minimalist Program (1990s–) asks: what is the most economical design for language? It strips syntax down to a single operation, Merge, which combines two elements into a new set. All phrase structure follows from Merge applying recursively.

The poverty of the stimulus argument: children produce complex grammatical sentences they have never heard, and they do not make certain predictable errors even when input would allow them. They know that 'Is the man who is tall happy?' is the correct question form (not *'Is the man who tall is happy?'). This sensitivity to structure — not just linear order — suggests innate syntactic knowledge.

Critics (construction grammarians, usage-based theorists) argue that rich input and general learning mechanisms can explain acquisition without UG.
